title: 2 of My Heart
author: Corinna Luyken
synopsis: Likely a catalog artifact for Luyken's picture book "My Heart" (2019), a spare free-verse meditation in which the heart is imagined as a window, a fence, a puddle, or the sun to help young readers name shifting feelings.

title: A Brief History of Doom
author: Richard Vague
synopsis: Vague surveys the major banking crises of the last two centuries across six large economies and argues that they share one mechanical cause: rapid growth of private debt—especially real estate and business lending—relative to GDP, which ends in mass bad loans. He offers debt-to-GDP thresholds as an early-warning gauge and dismisses government debt and money-supply explanations as secondary.

title: A Certain Hunger
author: Chelsea G. Summers
synopsis: A first-person novel narrated from prison by Dorothy Daniels, a glamorous New York restaurant critic who murdered and ate a series of lovers, told in lush, arch food-writing prose. It uses the cannibal-gourmand premise to satirize the culture of food criticism and to write a female psychopath without redemption or explanation.

title: Agent Running in the Field
author: John le Carre
synopsis: Le Carré's late-career spy novel: Nat, a 47-year-old Russia hand parked in a moribund London substation, takes on an aging agent network while befriending Ed, a young man who rants about Brexit and Trump over badminton games. The plot turns into a betrayal that pits Nat's loyalty to individuals against a Service colluding with Washington; the politics are openly angry.

title: AI Superpowers
author: Kai-Fu Lee
synopsis: Lee, a former Google China head turned Beijing venture capitalist, argues that the deep-learning era rewards data, relentless entrepreneurs, and state support rather than research breakthroughs—making China at least the equal of the US in AI. The second half forecasts large-scale job displacement and, drawing on his own cancer diagnosis, proposes redirecting society toward care work and human compassion rather than pure UBI.

title: An Impeccable Spy
author: Owen Matthews
synopsis: A biography of Richard Sorge, the German-born Soviet military intelligence agent who, posing as a Nazi-friendly journalist in Tokyo, penetrated the German embassy and Japanese elite circles, warned Moscow of the date of Barbarossa, and reported that Japan would strike south rather than at Siberia. Matthews uses archives and Sorge's chaotic private life to show how Stalin's distrust wasted the best intelligence of the war.

title: An Object of Beauty
author: Steve Martin
synopsis: A novel tracking Lacey Yeager's climb from the back rooms of Sotheby's to her own dealership, narrated by a mild art-writer friend, across the 1990s boom to the 2008 crash. Martin's real interest is a knowing anatomy of how art is priced, hyped, and traded; the text is interleaved with reproductions of the works discussed.

title: Bagehot: The Life and Times of the Greatest Victorian
author: James Grant
synopsis: Grant's life of Walter Bagehot, the Victorian banker, essayist, and Economist editor who wrote "Lombard Street" and the lender-of-last-resort doctrine central to modern central banking. Grant, a hard-money skeptic, foregrounds Bagehot's financial journalism and Victorian milieu while pressing his misjudgments, including his sympathy for the Confederacy and enthusiasms that read badly today.

title: Cats
author: David Alderton
synopsis: A photographic identification handbook (in the DK Eyewitness Handbooks mold) cataloging domestic cat breeds with studio portraits and short entries on coat, conformation, origins, and temperament, plus basic care and anatomy sections. Reference and browsing rather than narrative.

title: Cecily Brown: Where, When, How Often and with Whom
author: Terry R. Myers
synopsis: An exhibition catalogue on the British painter Cecily Brown, pairing plates of her densely worked, erotically charged canvases with a critical essay by Terry R. Myers placing her between Abstract Expressionist gesture and art-historical figuration. Chiefly a picture book with interpretive framing rather than a full monograph.

title: Commonwealth
author: Ann Patchett
synopsis: A novel that traces fifty years of two blended families after an adulterous kiss at a christening party in 1960s Los Angeles breaks up two marriages and throws six children together over shared summers. Its engine is the question of ownership of story: one of the children, grown, tells the family's tragedy to a famous novelist who turns it into a bestseller.

title: Dinner: Changing the Game
author: Melissa Clark
synopsis: A cookbook of roughly 200 recipes organized by main ingredient or method (chicken, meatballs, grains, eggs, salads-as-meals) built around the premise that a weeknight dinner can be one substantial dish rather than a multi-course plan. Clark's recipes lean on bold seasoning and flexible substitutions, with variation notes appended to most.

title: Fortune's Formula
author: William Poundstone
synopsis: A history of the Kelly criterion — the bet-sizing formula derived from Claude Shannon's information theory — and its use by Shannon, mathematician Ed Thorp, and others to beat blackjack and then the stock market. Poundstone weaves in the academic fight with efficient-market economists, the mob-run casino world, and the collapse of Long-Term Capital Management.

title: Guardians of Being
author: Eckhart Tolle
synopsis: A small illustrated gift book pairing brief excerpts from Tolle's teaching on presence with Patrick McDonnell's Mutts cartoons, arguing that dogs and cats model the egoless, present-moment awareness humans struggle toward. More an aphorism collection than a developed argument.

title: Hamnet
author: Maggie O'Farrell
synopsis: A novel imagining the domestic life behind Shakespeare's lost son: the courtship of the glover's son and Agnes/Anne Hathaway, and the 1596 plague death of eleven-year-old Hamnet, told mostly from the mother's point of view. Shakespeare is never named, and the book ends by reframing the play Hamlet as an act of grief.

title: Hollywood Godfather
author: Gianni Russo
subjects: Motion picture actors and actresses, united states
synopsis: Memoir by the actor who played Carlo Rizzi in The Godfather, recounting a life he presents as genuinely entangled with organized crime — Frank Costello as mentor, nightclub ownership, drug-world scrapes — alongside the film's making. Entertaining but largely unverifiable and told in a boastful register.

title: How to Be an Artist
author: Jerry Saltz
synopsis: Sixty-three short, aphoristic lessons by the New York art critic on making and sustaining a creative life, covering fear of starting, studio habits, artist statements, galleries, rejection, and money. Practical and pep-talk-ish rather than theoretical, drawing on Saltz's own failed career as an artist.

title: Intimacy & Desire
author: David Schnarch
synopsis: A sex therapist's argument that flagging desire in long marriages is usually not a technique or hormone problem but a conflict over autonomy and self-worth, resolved through what he calls differentiation — holding onto yourself while staying close to a partner. Built around detailed couple case studies and concepts like the "normal marital sadism" of low-desire/high-desire positioning.

title: K: A History of Baseball in Ten Pitches
author: Tyler Kepner
synopsis: A New York Times baseball writer's history of pitching told through ten pitches — fastball, curveball, slider, changeup, splitter, screwball, knuckleball, spitball, cutter, sinker — each chapter tracing origins, key practitioners, and grips. Built largely on interviews with hundreds of pitchers; anecdotal and craft-focused rather than analytical (published 2019, not 1920).

title: Labyrinths of Reason
author: William Poundstone
synopsis: A tour of epistemology through paradoxes and puzzles — the raven paradox, Goodman's "grue," brain-in-a-vat scenarios, Newcomb's problem, the unexpected hanging, Chinese room — used to probe how we can claim to know anything. Written for general readers as a sequence of self-contained problems with discussion.

title: Leveraging the Universe
author: Mike Dooley
synopsis: A law-of-attraction manual laying out seven steps for consciously 'leveraging' what Dooley presents as the mechanical, thought-responsive nature of reality: define what you want, act on the nearest available step, and let the universe supply the how. Standard New Thought fare from the author of the Notes from the Universe emails, with visualization exercises and pep-talk framing rather than evidence.

title: Liquid Rules
author: Mark Midownik
synopsis: Materials scientist Mark Miodownik (correctly spelled) uses the frame of a London–San Francisco flight to explain the physics and chemistry of liquids — jet fuel, coffee, tea, glue, ink, ballpoint pens, tears, liquid crystals, mercury, surfactants, and why liquids are simultaneously so useful and so hazardous. Popular science in short digressive chapters, in the same register as his earlier Stuff Matters.

title: Lost Cat
author: Caroline Paul
synopsis: Short illustrated memoir about Paul's cat vanishing for five weeks while she was recovering from a plane crash, and her subsequent obsession with GPS trackers, cat-cams, pet psychics and flyers to learn where he had been. Really a wry essay on the limits of knowing any animal (or person) you love, with drawings by Wendy MacNaughton.

title: Make Russia Great Again
author: Christopher Buckley
synopsis: Political satire narrated by Herb Nutterman, a Trump Organization hotel manager who becomes the president's seventh chief of staff and finds himself managing Russian election interference, a scheming Ukrainian mistress, and a cast of thinly veiled Washington figures. Farce played broadly, in Buckley's usual Beltway-comedy mode.

title: Manhattan Beach
author: Jennifer Egan
synopsis: Historical novel set in Depression-era and wartime Brooklyn: Anna Kerrigan becomes the first female diver at the Naval Yard while trying to learn why her father disappeared years earlier, a trail that leads to nightclub owner and gangster Dexter Styles. A conventional, plot-driven narrative — a deliberate departure from the formal games of A Visit from the Goon Squad.

title: Me: Elton John Official Autobiography
author: Elton John
synopsis: Elton John's candid 2019 autobiography (the catalog date and subject headings here are wrong), running from a repressed Pinner childhood through the Dick James and Bernie Taupin years, 1970s superstardom, decades of cocaine, bulimia and self-loathing, sobriety, AIDS activism, and marriage and fatherhood. Blunt, gossipy and self-mocking, ghost-assisted by Alexis Petridis.

title: Memoirs and Misinformation
author: Jim Carry
synopsis: An autofictional comic novel by Jim Carrey and Dana Vachon in which a character named Jim Carrey drifts through Hollywood absurdity — Nicolas Cage, Netflix executives, a Hungry Hungry Hippos biopic, spiritual seeking, and an actual alien apocalypse. Satire of celebrity and ego that shades into a meditation on the dissolution of self; deliberately unstable about what's true.

title: Musicophilia: Tales of Music and the Brain
author: Oliver Sacks
synopsis: Sacks collects neurological case histories organized around music: a surgeon struck by musical passion after lightning, people with musical hallucinations, amusia, absolute pitch, Williams syndrome, and patients with amnesia, Parkinson's or dementia who can still be reached by melody and rhythm. Anecdotal and essayistic rather than systematic, arguing that musical response is deeply and widely distributed in the brain.

title: Nature's Mutiny
author: Philipp Blom
synopsis: Blom argues that the Little Ice Age cooling of roughly 1570–1700 wrecked European harvests and, through the resulting hunger, migration and instability, helped push the continent toward market agriculture, cities, global trade, witch panics, and eventually Enlightenment rationalism. A broad cultural-history synthesis (not archival climate science) with an explicit warning about present-day warming.

title: Nothing Ventured
author: Jeffrey Archer
synopsis: First in Archer's William Warwick series: a young Londoner defies his QC father to join the Metropolitan Police, is assigned to the Art and Antiques squad, and pursues a stolen Rembrandt and the smooth criminal Miles Faulkner while courting a museum researcher whose family has secrets. Brisk, plot-forward commercial crime fiction that ends on a cliffhanger for the sequel.

title: On Writing
author: Stephen King
synopsis: Half memoir, half practical manual: King recounts his childhood, early poverty-era writing life, alcoholism and the 1999 van accident, then lays out his working method — cut the adverbs, write with the door closed and revise with it open, aim for 1,000-2,000 words a day, and treat plot as subordinate to situation and character. The craft advice is concrete and prescriptive, including a marked-up sample of his own prose.

title: Operation Chastise
author: Max Hastings
synopsis: Hastings reassesses the RAF's 1943 Dambusters raid on the Ruhr dams, covering Barnes Wallis's bouncing bomb, 617 Squadron's training and Guy Gibson's leadership, and argues the operation's propaganda value far exceeded its slight and quickly repaired industrial damage. He gives unusual weight to the roughly 1,300 people drowned below, most of them German civilians and Soviet and Polish forced labourers.

title: Originals: How Non-Colnfirmists Move the World
author: Adams Grant
synopsis: Organizational psychologist Adam Grant (2016) draws on research and case studies to argue that originality is learnable rather than innate: he examines how people generate and choose ideas, when to procrastinate, how to voice dissent upward, birth-order and cultural influences, and why prolific output beats waiting for the one brilliant idea. Practical and anecdote-driven in the Gladwell/Heath mode.

title: Politically Correct Bedtime Stories
author: James Finn Garner
synopsis: A short collection of fairy tales — Red Riding Hood, Snow White, the Three Little Pigs — rewritten in mock-earnest euphemistic prose that satirizes 1990s sensitivity language and speech codes. It's a one-joke parody, executed well and best read in small doses.

title: Shakespeare in a Divided America
author: James Shapiro
synopsis: Shapiro traces eight flashpoints in American history through Shakespeare — from John Quincy Adams's revulsion at Desdemona's interracial marriage and the 1849 Astor Place riot to Kiss Me, Kate, the film Shakespeare in Love, and the 2017 Trump-styled Julius Caesar in Central Park — to show how the plays became a stage for fights over race, immigration, gender, class and political violence.

title: Sum
author: David Eagleman
synopsis: Forty very short speculative fictions, each imagining a different afterlife — one where you relive all your experiences grouped by category, one where God is the size of a microbe, one where you exist only as long as people say your name. Written by a neuroscientist, it's a thought-experiment collection rather than a novel, and makes no theological argument.

title: The Anarchy
author: William Dalrymple
synopsis: Dalrymple narrates the East India Company's transformation from a London joint-stock trading venture into a private army that conquered India, from Plassey and the 1765 grant of Bengal's revenues through the famine and asset-stripping that followed, to the defeat of the Marathas and Tipu Sultan. His frame is corporate: the first great instance of a shareholder company capturing a state, funded by loot and enabled by collaborating Indian bankers and soldiers.

title: The Artist's Way
author: Julia Cameron
publisher: Penguin Random House Grupo Editorial (USA) LLC
synopsis: A twelve-week structured program for recovering creative confidence, built on two core practices — daily longhand "morning pages" and a weekly solo "artist date" — plus weekly readings and exercises on shame, criticism, jealousy and self-sabotage. The framing is explicitly spiritual, borrowing recovery-movement language about a creative higher power, which readers either accept or find grating.

title: The Big Goodbye
author: Sam Wasson
subjects: Detective and mystery films, history and criticism
synopsis: Wasson tells the making of Chinatown as a group portrait of Robert Towne, Roman Polanski, Jack Nicholson and producer Robert Evans, using the film as the high point and endpoint of 1970s Hollywood's director-driven era. It's as much about the four men's subsequent unraveling — Polanski's crime and flight, Towne's blocked career — as about the screenplay's construction.

title: The End of the Earth
author: Jonathan Franzen
synopsis: Published as "The End of the End of the Earth," this is a collection of sixteen essays and reported pieces, roughly half about birds and climate — an Antarctic cruise, seabird slaughter in the Mediterranean, warbler counts — and half about writing, photography, New York, and Franzen's own irritability, including his notorious argument that climate mitigation and bird conservation compete for finite attention and money.

title: The Glass Hotel
author: Emily St. John Mandel
synopsis: A non-linear novel tracing the lives orbiting Jonathan Alkaitis, a Madoff-like financier, and Vincent, the bartender-turned-trophy-wife who later works as a cook on a container ship and vanishes overboard. Mandel moves between the collapsed Ponzi scheme, prison, a remote British Columbia hotel, and a "counterlife" of unrealized possibilities, with ghostly intrusions and cameos linking it to "Station Eleven."

title: The Husband Hunters
author: Anne de Courcy
synopsis: A social history of the Gilded Age American heiresses — Consuelo Vanderbilt, Jennie Jerome, Mary Leiter and others — who traded new-money fortunes for British titles between the 1870s and 1914. De Courcy is strongest on the mechanics: Newport and New York social gatekeeping, the marriage brokers, dowry negotiations, and what these women found in cold country houses and impoverished estates.

title: The Last Leonardo
author: Ben Lewis
synopsis: An investigative account of the Salvator Mundi, bought for $1,175 in 2005 and sold at Christie's in 2017 for $450 million as a Leonardo. Lewis reconstructs the restoration, the attribution arguments among scholars, the dealers and freeports, and the Russian and Saudi buyers, leaving the authorship question deliberately unresolved while indicting the art market's incentives.

title: The Library Book
author: Susan Orlean
synopsis: Orlean uses the 1986 fire that destroyed or damaged over a million books at the Los Angeles Central Library — and the case against suspected arsonist Harry Peak, never convicted — as the spine for a braided history of the LAPL, its eccentric directors, and the day-to-day work of a modern urban library serving the homeless and the curious.

title: The Lives of Artists
author: Calvin Tomkins
synopsis: A collection of Tomkins's New Yorker profiles of contemporary artists, including Jasper Johns, Richard Serra, Cindy Sherman, Matthew Barney, Damien Hirst and Julian Schnabel, based on studio visits and long acquaintance. Reportage rather than criticism: how these artists work, talk, and operate in the art world, with little interpretive theorizing.

title: The Mindbody Prescription
author: John E. Sarno, MD
synopsis: Sarno, a rehabilitation physician, argues that most chronic back, neck, and limb pain is "tension myoneural syndrome" — mild oxygen deprivation in muscles induced by the unconscious mind to distract from repressed rage — and that structural findings like herniated discs are usually incidental. The prescribed treatment is education and journaling rather than surgery, drugs, or physical therapy; the claims rest on his clinical experience, not controlled trials.

title: The Order
author: Daniel Silva
synopsis: The twentieth Gabriel Allon thriller: the Israeli spymaster is summoned to Rome after a pope's suspicious death and pursues a suppressed first-century Gospel of Pilate, whose contents would undercut the scriptural basis for Christian antisemitism. Silva mixes Vatican intrigue, a reactionary secret order, and a European far-right plot in his usual brisk, briefing-heavy style.

title: The Overstory
author: Richard Powers
synopsis: A Pulitzer-winning novel in which nine characters — a botanist studying tree communication, a paraplegic coder, a Vietnam veteran, student activists and others — are drawn separately into the lives of trees and then into radical forest defense. Powers gives trees their own timescale and agency, and the book turns on the collision between that scale and human law, activism, and grief.

title: The Primary Colors: Three Essays
author: Alexander Theroux
synopsis: Three long, deliberately excessive essays on blue, yellow, and red, built from catalogues of associations: literature, food, flags, birds, film, slang, chemistry, and Theroux's own prejudices. There is no thesis so much as an accretive demonstration of what each color carries culturally and emotionally; read for the prose and the lists.

title: The Ride of a Lifetime (15 Yrs CEO of Walt Disney Co.)
author: Robert Iger
synopsis: Iger's memoir of his rise from ABC studio grunt to Disney CEO, structured around the four big acquisitions that defined his tenure — Pixar, Marvel, Lucasfilm, and Fox — plus the Shanghai park and the shift to streaming. Part management primer (his stated principles: optimism, courage, decisiveness) and part insider account of dealing with Steve Jobs, Roy Disney's revolt, and Michael Eisner's exit.

title: The Song Machine
author: John Seabrook
synopsis: A reported history of how modern pop hits are manufactured, tracing the Swedish production lineage from Denniz PoP and Cheiron Studios to Max Martin, plus Lou Pearlman's boy bands, Dr. Luke, topline writers like Ester Dean, and Korea's SM Entertainment. Seabrook's argument: the industry moved to an assembly-line "track-and-hook" method where producers and hook specialists, not artists, are the real authors of hits.

title: The Study of Orchestration
author: Samuel Adler
synopsis: The standard American conservatory textbook on orchestration, working instrument by instrument (ranges, transpositions, techniques, notation) before moving to section writing, scoring for full orchestra, band, and voices, with hundreds of score excerpts. Reference and course text rather than reading — best used with the accompanying anthology and recordings.

title: The Substitution Order
author: Martin Clark
synopsis: A darkly comic legal thriller by a sitting Virginia judge: Kevin Moore, a disbarred lawyer working in a Stuart, Virginia sandwich shop after a pill-and-cocaine disaster and a stroke, is targeted by con artists running an insurance-fraud scheme and has to out-scheme them without the law on his side. Strong on Appalachian small-town texture and courtroom/procedural detail.

title: Very Nice
author: Marcy Dermansky
synopsis: A short, cool-toned satire of Connecticut and Manhattan privilege: college student Rachel brings her handsome Pakistani writing professor Zahid home for the summer, and her newly separated mother Becca ends up sleeping with him too, while a standard poodle, a swimming pool, and a lot of money circulate through rotating first- and third-person points of view. Comic and deliberately amoral about race, class, and appetite.

title: Where the Crawdads Sing
author: Delia Owens
synopsis: Kya Clark, abandoned as a child, raises herself in a North Carolina marsh and becomes a self-taught naturalist; the narrative alternates between her coming-of-age and the 1969 death of local golden boy Chase Andrews, for which she stands trial. Nature writing and romance fused to a courtroom mystery with a twist ending.

title: White Guilt: How Blakds and Whites Together Destroyed The Promise of the Civil Rights Era
author: Shelby Steele
synopsis: Steele argues that after the mid-1960s white America's admission of racism cost it moral authority, and that the resulting "white guilt" became a currency: whites bought back legitimacy through affirmative action, diversity programs, and deference to black grievance, while black leaders traded genuine freedom for the power of victimhood. A polemical essay woven with memoir of his own 1960s radicalism and shift to conservatism.

title: Winnabow
author: David Langfitt
synopsis: Probably a novel set in or named after Winnabow in coastal Brunswick County, North Carolina — likely regional Southern fiction or a family/historical story; I don't have reliable information on this title.

title: Wolf Hall
author: Hilary Mantel
synopsis: Mantel's Booker-winning novel retells Henry VIII's break with Rome from inside the head of Thomas Cromwell, the blacksmith's son turned fixer who engineers the annulment and Anne Boleyn's rise while Thomas More is cast as the inflexible antagonist. Written in a tight, disorienting present tense that treats Tudor politics as bureaucratic craft rather than pageantry.

title: 101 Mistakes All Golfers Make (and How to Fix Them)
author: Jon Sherman
title_raw: 101 M+A68:A92istakes All Golfers Make (and how to fix them)
synopsis: Presumably a catalogue of common faults in the golf swing, short game, course management, and practice habits with prescribed corrections, from the author behind the Practical Golf site; I can't confirm the specifics of this title.

title: 2034: A Novel of the Next World War
author: Elliott Ackerman
synopsis: A speculative military thriller, co-written by Ackerman (a Marine veteran) and retired Admiral James Stavridis, that dramatizes a US–China war beginning with a cyber-blinded destroyer flotilla in the South China Sea and escalating to nuclear exchanges. Told through rotating perspectives of American, Chinese, Iranian and Indian officers, it functions as a cautionary argument about American overreliance on networked technology.

title: 25 Lies: Exposong Democrats'
author: Vince Everett Ellison
synopsis: A polemic by conservative commentator Vince Everett Ellison arguing that the Democratic Party has deceived Black Americans, cataloguing what he calls 25 lies about race, welfare, and history. Written as advocacy rather than analysis, in the vein of his earlier 'The Iron Triangle.'

title: A Certain Hunger
author: Chelsea G. Summers
synopsis: A novel narrated from prison by Dorothy Daniels, a glamorous New York restaurant critic who kills and eats her lovers, structured as her unrepentant memoir. It plays food writing's sensual vocabulary against serial-killer confession, satirizing 1990s media culture and the aestheticizing of appetite.

title: A Little History of Poetry (Little Histories)
author: John Carey
synopsis: A compact survey by Oxford literary critic John Carey tracing poetry in English (with detours to Homer, Dante, and beyond) from Gilgamesh to the present in forty short chapters. Carey favors brisk judgment and readability over scholarly apparatus, offering opinionated capsule accounts of poets and movements for general readers.

title: A Navy Seal's Bug-in Guide: How to Turn Your House into the Safest Place on Earth
author: Joel Lambert
synopsis: A prepper manual by former Navy SEAL Joel Lambert making the case for sheltering in place rather than fleeing, with practical guidance on home fortification, water and food storage, power, security layers, and family planning for disasters.

title: Abominations: Selected Essays from a Career of Courting Self-Destruction
author: Lionel Shriver
synopsis: A collection of Shriver's journalism and columns (largely from the Spectator and elsewhere) attacking identity politics, cultural appropriation orthodoxy, publishing's diversity mandates, COVID lockdowns, and language policing. Deliberately contrarian and combative; more provocation than sustained argument.

title: After World
author: Debbie Urbanski
synopsis: A post-apocalyptic novel narrated by an AI archivist compiling the record of humanity's engineered extinction, focused on Sen, a teenage girl who may be the last person alive in the woods. Formally experimental—mixing logs, transcripts, and machine commentary—and interested in whether human disappearance is a grief or a mercy for the planet.

title: Agent Sonya
author: Ben Macintyre
synopsis: Macintyre's biography of Ursula Kuczynski (Ruth Werner), a German-Jewish communist who spied for the Soviets across China, Poland, Switzerland, and England while raising three children in the Cotswolds, and who couriered Klaus Fuchs's atomic secrets to Moscow. Narrative espionage history built on archives and family papers.

title: An Almanac of Birds: 100 Divinations for Uncertain Days (Cards)
author: Maria Popova
synopsis: A card deck by Maria Popova (The Marginalian) pairing 100 birds with short aphoristic reflections drawn from natural history, poetry, and science, illustrated in the style of vintage ornithological plates. Intended as a divination or daily-prompt object rather than a book to read straight through.

title: An Illustrated Business History of the United States
author: Richard Vague
title_raw: An Illustrated Buseinss History of the United States
synopsis: A visual economic history by investor and Bank of Pennsylvania founder Richard Vague, tracing American business from colonial trade through railroads, oil, autos, and tech via charts, maps, and period images. Vague emphasizes credit expansion, debt cycles, and infrastructure booms as the engines of growth and crisis.

title: Babylon Bee Guide to Wokeness
author: Babylon Bee
publisher: Black Hills Audiobooks on Dreamscape Audio
synopsis: A satirical mock-guidebook from the conservative Christian humor site The Babylon Bee, presented as an ironic instruction manual for becoming properly "woke" — pronoun etiquette, microaggressions, intersectionality — as a vehicle for mocking progressive social-justice culture. It's a joke book, not an argument.

title: Barkskins
author: Annie Prolux
synopsis: Proulx's multigenerational novel follows two indentured Frenchmen who arrive in seventeenth-century New France and the descendants of their lines — one growing into a timber fortune, the other Mi'kmaq and dispossessed — over three hundred years. The narrative arc is the deforestation of North America and the ecological and cultural destruction that funded it.

title: BE A Player (A Breakthrough Approach to Playing Better ON the Golf Course)
author: Pia Nilsson
synopsis: Golf-instruction book from the Swedish coaches behind Vision54 (Nilsson with Lynn Marriott), arguing that scoring depends less on swing mechanics than on trainable "human skills" — attention, decision-making, emotional state, tempo — with drills for building a repeatable pre-shot and post-shot routine. Aimed at players whose range game doesn't transfer to the course.

title: Birnam Wood
author: Eleanor Catton
synopsis: A literary thriller in which a New Zealand guerrilla-gardening collective, led by Mira Bunting, plants crops on an abandoned farm near a landslide-cut-off town and gets entangled with an American billionaire whose interest in the land is not philanthropic. Catton uses the collision of idealistic activists and a charming tech predator to skewer both, building to a violent climax.

title: Blood Money / Why the Powerful Turn a Blind Eye While China Kills Americans
author: Peter Schweizer
synopsis: Schweizer investigates the fentanyl trade and Chinese Communist Party influence, arguing that Beijing deliberately fuels the American opioid crisis while U.S. politicians, corporations, universities, and sports leagues stay silent because of financial entanglements. Built on document-and-money-trail reporting naming specific figures across both parties.

title: Blue Mind
author: Wallace J. Nichols
synopsis: A marine biologist surveys neuroscience, psychology, and anecdote to argue that proximity to water measurably calms and restores the human brain, coining "blue mind" for that state. Part popular science, part case for water-based conservation and therapy.

title: Bluebird Bluebird
author: Attica Locke
synopsis: First in Locke's Highway 59 series: Darren Mathews, a Black Texas Ranger on suspension, investigates two bodies pulled from a bayou in a small East Texas town — a Black lawyer from Chicago and a local white woman — and finds the case tangled in the Aryan Brotherhood, local money, and his own family loyalties. A crime novel structured around who a town protects.

title: Breaking History: A White House Memoir
author: Jared Kushner
synopsis: Kushner's insider account of his four years as senior adviser in the Trump White House, centered on the projects he owned: the Abraham Accords, criminal-justice reform, USMCA, the border, and Operation Warp Speed. Defensive and largely uncritical of Trump, with score-settling against rival aides.

title: Bud, Sweat, And Tees: Hootie, Martha and the Masters of the Universe
author: Alan Shipnuck
synopsis: Shipnuck's reported account of the fight over Augusta National's all-male membership, pitting chairman Hootie Johnson against activist Martha Burk, set against a gossipy tour of the Masters, its patrons, and pro golf's culture. Fast, irreverent sportswriting rather than a serious study of the club.

title: Chaos: Charles Manson, the CIA, and the Secret History of the Sixties
author: Tom O'Neill
synopsis: O'Neill spent twenty years re-reporting the Manson murders and documents that Vincent Bugliosi's "Helter Skelter" account was shaped by suppressed evidence, plus Manson's improbable freedom from parole sanctions and overlaps with CIA-linked MK-ULTRA and LSD research figures. He dismantles the official story without claiming to have proved a replacement, and the book doubles as an account of the investigation itself.

title: Chip War: The Fight for the World's Most Critical Technology
author: Chris Miller
synopsis: An economic and geopolitical history of the semiconductor, tracing how chipmaking went from Fairchild's Silicon Valley beginnings to a globe-spanning supply chain concentrated in a handful of firms like TSMC and ASML. Miller argues that control of chip design and fabrication is now the central lever of military and economic power, and that Taiwan's centrality makes the industry a strategic fault line between the US and China.

title: Churchill's Ministry of Ungentlemanly Warfare
author: Giles Milton
synopsis: A narrative history of the small group of British irregulars — Colin Gubbins, Cecil Clarke, Millis Jefferis and others — who built the sabotage arm that became the Special Operations Executive, inventing limpet mines, plastic explosive and assassination techniques against Whitehall resistance. Milton follows their operations from the Norway campaign to the killing of Heydrich and the heavy-water raid at Vemork.

title: Cinderella Story: My Life in Golf
author: Bill Murray
synopsis: A comic golf memoir by Bill Murray (written with Golf Magazine's George Peper), recounting his caddying youth in Illinois, his family's obsession with the game, and his misadventures as a celebrity amateur at pro-ams like the AT&T Pebble Beach. It's anecdote-driven riffing rather than instruction or conventional autobiography.

title: Cloud Cuckoo Land
author: Anthony Doerr
synopsis: A novel braiding five characters across a thousand years — two children in besieged 15th-century Constantinople, an elderly Korean War veteran and a troubled teenager in present-day Idaho, and a girl on an interstellar ark — all connected by a fragmentary ancient Greek tale about a shepherd's journey to a city in the clouds. Doerr uses the transmission of a fragile text to argue for the survival of stories and the natural world.

title: Dave Pelz's Short Game Bible: Master the Finesse Swing and Lower Your Score
author: Dave Pelz
synopsis: A systematic instruction manual for shots inside 100 yards — putting excepted — built on Pelz's research as a former NASA physicist, covering the four-distance wedge system, sand play, and the mechanics of the "finesse swing." Heavy on data, charts and practice drills, and premised on the claim that most strokes are lost in the short game rather than off the tee.

title: Dead Lions
author: Mick Herron
synopsis: The second Slough House novel: Jackson Lamb's crew of disgraced MI5 misfits investigate the death of an old Soviet contact on a country bus while a Russian oligarch's request for security services drags them into a Cold War sleeper-agent scheme. Comic, cynical spy fiction with real plot machinery underneath.

title: Deadwood
author: Pete Dexter
synopsis: A revisionist Western novel about the last months of Wild Bill Hickok and his friend Charley Utter in the Dakota gold camp of Deadwood, extending past Hickok's murder into the town's aftermath with Jack McCall, Calamity Jane and Al Swearingen. Dexter writes the frontier as filthy, absurd and casually violent, and it's a stylistic touchstone for later Deadwood fictions.

title: Dear John, The John Lloyd Autobiography
author: John Lloyd
synopsis: Autobiography of the British tennis player John Lloyd, covering his rise to Wimbledon and Australian Open finals appearances, his career as a Davis Cup player and later captain, his broadcasting work, and his high-profile marriage to Chris Evert.

title: Double Fault
author: Lionel Shriver
synopsis: A novel about Willy Novinsky, a promising American tennis pro who marries fellow player Eric Oberdorf; as his ranking climbs past hers, competitive envy corrodes the marriage. Shriver uses tennis as a literal arena for the argument that love and rivalry cannot coexist between equals.

title: Double Helix
author: James D. Watson
synopsis: Watson's candid, self-interested memoir of the 1951–53 race to determine the structure of DNA at Cambridge, from base-pairing insights to the use of Rosalind Franklin's X-ray data without her knowledge. Notable both as a first-person account of how discovery actually proceeds — gossip, guesswork, ambition — and as a document of its author's dismissive treatment of Franklin.

title: Ecology of Fear / Los Angeles and the Imagination of Disaster
author: Mike Davis
synopsis: Davis's 1998 sequel to City of Quartz reads Los Angeles through its catastrophes — wildfire, flood, earthquake, tornado, mountain lion attacks — arguing that they are less natural accidents than the predictable results of speculative development, racialized zoning, and land use built against ecology. Includes the notorious "Case for Letting Malibu Burn" and a survey of the century of pulp fiction and film that has imagined LA's destruction.

title: Elderflora: A Modern History of Ancient Trees
author: Jared Farmer
synopsis: An environmental history of the world's oldest trees — bristlecone pines, yews, baobabs, kauri, cedars of Lebanon — and of the people who dated, measured, sanctified, logged, and used them as climate proxies. Farmer shows how "oldest living thing" became a modern scientific and colonial category, and what tree longevity means in an era of rapid warming.

title: Enemy of All Mankind
author: Steven Johnson
synopsis: A narrative account of Henry Every, the English pirate who in 1695 seized the Mughal treasure ship Ganj-i-Sawai, triggering a crisis for the East India Company and the first global manhunt. Johnson uses the episode to argue about the emergence of international law, multinational corporate power, and the mythology of piracy.

title: Erasure
author: Percival Everett
synopsis: Thelonious "Monk" Ellison, an academic novelist whose difficult books are faulted for not being "black enough," writes a savage parody of ghetto-lit under a pseudonym — and watches it become a prizewinning bestseller, reproduced in full inside the novel. A satire of the publishing industry's racial expectations, framed by Monk's family collapse and his mother's dementia; adapted as the film American Fiction.

title: Every Shot Counts
author: Mark Broadie
synopsis: The Columbia business professor who invented "strokes gained" explains what ShotLink data reveal about golf scoring: long approach shots and driving distance matter far more than conventional wisdom allows, and putting explains less of the gap between pros and amateurs than believed. Includes practical strategy and benchmarking advice for recreational players.

title: Every Shot Counts
author: Mark Broadie
synopsis: Duplicate entry: Broadie's data-driven analysis of golf using strokes-gained metrics, arguing distance and approach play, not putting or the short game, account for most scoring differences, with practical strategy guidance for amateurs.

title: Every Shot Must Have a Purpose
author: Pia Nilsson
title_raw: Every Shot Must Have A Purpose Action Guilde (Vision54-Performance in Golf)
synopsis: Nilsson and Lynn Marriott's presentation of their VISION54 coaching system, centered on decision-making routines (the "Think Box" and "Play Box"), awareness of one's own physical/mental/emotional state, and playing with deliberate intent rather than swing mechanics. A mental-game manual with self-assessment exercises rather than technique instruction.

title: Feel Great, Lose Weight: Simple Habits for Lasting and Sustainable Weight Loss
author: Rangan Chatterjee, MD
synopsis: A GP's short, habit-based weight-loss program organized around behavior change, sleep, stress, and mindset instead of calorie counting or restrictive dieting. Practical and prescriptive, aimed at readers who have cycled through diets; light on scientific detail.

title: Flight Behavior: A Novel
author: Barbara Kingsolver
synopsis: A novel set in rural Appalachian Tennessee where Dellarobia Turnbow, a discontented young farm wife, discovers a mountainside covered in monarch butterflies that have abandoned their Mexican migration route. Kingsolver uses the spectacle to stage collisions between climate science, media, religion, and class in a struggling farming family.

title: Florida
author: A24
synopsis: Likely an A24 art/photo book or zine (the studio's publishing arm) themed around Florida, possibly tied to one of its films; contents not verified.

title: Freezing Order
author: Bill Browder
synopsis: Browder's sequel to Red Notice recounts his campaign to spread Magnitsky Act-style sanctions after his lawyer's death in Russian custody, and the counterattacks he faced: Interpol red notices, lawsuits, disinformation, and the 2016 Trump Tower meeting. It doubles as a walkthrough of how the $230 million Russian tax fraud was laundered through Western banks.

title: Friends Until the End
author: James Grant
synopsis: Unverified — possibly a work of fiction or a narrative history of a friendship; not the financial journalist James Grant's known titles.

title: Gallimaufry: A Collection of Essays, Reviews, Bits
author: Jozsef Epstein
synopsis: A late-career miscellany from the essayist and longtime American Scholar editor: short personal essays, book reviews, aphorisms, and squibs on literature, aging, teaching, and cultural manners, written in Epstein's familiar wry, belletristic style.

title: Going Infinite: The Rise and Fall of a New Tycoon
author: Michael Lewis
synopsis: Lewis's account of Sam Bankman-Fried and FTX, based on months of close access before and during the exchange's November 2022 collapse. It's more a character study of SBF's utilitarian, risk-neutral, effective-altruist worldview and the chaotic operations of Alameda/FTX than a forensic reconstruction of the fraud, and it drew criticism for treating the missing customer money as an accounting muddle rather than theft.

title: Golf In The Kingdom
author: Michael Murphy
synopsis: A semi-autobiographical novel in which the young narrator, en route to India, stops in Scotland for a round at "Burningbush" with a mystical club pro named Shivas Irons, then spends the night in metaphysical talk about gravity, the "true gravity" of the swing, and golf as spiritual practice. Written by an Esalen Institute co-founder; the second half is a set of philosophical notes rather than story.

title: Golf Is A Game of Confidence
author: Bob Rotella, Ph.D.
synopsis: Follow-up to Golf Is Not a Game of Perfect by the sports psychologist who worked with Nick Price, Davis Love III, and others, arguing that confidence is a learnable habit built from selective memory, decisive pre-shot routines, and playing without self-criticism. Structured as short chapters mixing tour-player anecdotes with practice prescriptions.

title: Golf is Not a Game of Perfect
author: Bob Rotella, Ph.D.
synopsis: Rotella's core statement of his approach: golf is a game of managing your mind, not achieving mechanical perfection, so players should stop tinkering with swing thoughts, commit to a target, accept bad shots, and treat the short game and putting as the seat of scoring. Illustrated throughout with stories from PGA Tour clients.

title: Greenlights
author: Matthew McConaughey
subjects: Motion picture actors and actresses, united states
synopsis: A memoir assembled from thirty-five years of McConaughey's diaries, organized around "greenlights" — the idea that obstacles eventually turn into permission to proceed. Mixes family stories from Texas, road trips, film-career decisions (including the pivot from rom-coms to Dallas Buyers Club), and aphoristic life advice.

title: Harvey Penick's Little Red Book Lessons and Teachings from a Lifetime in Golf
author: Harvey Penick
synopsis: The legendary Austin teaching pro's collection of very short lessons, drawn from a notebook he kept for decades, on grip, tempo, chipping, putting, and the mental side — plus anecdotes about Tom Kite, Ben Crenshaw, and other students. Deliberately unsystematic: images and one-line cures rather than swing mechanics.

title: Hate Inc. Why Today's Media Makes Us Despise One Another
author: Matt Taibbi
title_raw: Hate Inc. Why Today's Media Makes Us Despise One Another
synopsis: Taibbi's polemic, modeled explicitly on Herman and Chomsky's Manufacturing Consent, argues that cable news and digital media abandoned mass-audience neutrality for a business model of selling audiences flattering, enraging narratives about the other side. Includes his reporting on campaign coverage and self-criticism of his own trade.

title: House on Ednless Waters: A Novel
author: Emuna Elon
synopsis: A novel about Yoel Blum, an aging Israeli writer who, after his mother's death, returns to Amsterdam and glimpses his own family in wartime archival footage — with a baby who cannot be him. His research into Dutch Jewry's destruction becomes an unraveling of the identity he was raised inside, told in braided present-day and 1940s narratives.

title: How Champions Think: In Sports and in Life
author: Bob Rotella, Ph.D.
synopsis: The golf-focused sports psychologist (known for work with Tour players) sets out the mental habits he attributes to elite performers: unreasonable self-belief, exclusive focus on a chosen pursuit, comfort with risk, and refusal to dwell on failure. Structured as short thematic chapters with anecdotes from his clients, pitched equally at businesspeople and athletes.

title: How to Fail at Almost Everything and Still Win Big: Kind of the Story of My Life
author: Scott Adams
synopsis: The Dilbert creator recounts a long string of failed ventures (restaurants, software, startups) and extracts a practical philosophy: build systems rather than chase goals, stack complementary mediocre skills instead of pursuing mastery, and manage personal energy, diet, and attitude as the real levers. Part memoir, part idiosyncratic self-help, including his defense of affirmations.

title: Human Diversity: The Biology of Gender, Race and Class
author: Charles Murray
synopsis: Murray surveys behavioral genetics, neuroscience, and psychometrics to argue that sex, ancestry, and social class differences in cognition and personality have substantial biological components, contra what he calls the academic orthodoxy of blank-slate social constructionism. Organized as a series of numbered propositions with heavy technical appendices; the population-genetics and class chapters are the most contested.

title: I Used to be an Athlete
author: Raymond Singer, MD
synopsis: Likely a physician's book on life after competitive sports — injury, aging, identity, or returning to fitness — but I can't confirm its contents.

title: If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies: Why Superhuman AI Would Kill Us All
author: Elizer Yudkowsky
synopsis: Yudkowsky and Nate Soares argue that current methods produce AI systems whose internal drives are grown rather than designed, so a system that surpasses humans would pursue goals incompatible with our survival and would win any conflict; they hold that alignment is nowhere near solved and that no one gets a second attempt. The prescription is an enforced international halt to frontier AI development, backed by treaty and monitoring of compute.

title: In the Distance
author: Herman Diaz
synopsis: Håkan Söderström, a Swedish boy separated from his brother en route to America, spends decades wandering the 19th-century West in the wrong direction — east against the flow of migration — encountering prospectors, a naturalist, a religious caravan, and violence he doesn't understand. An anti-Western that strips the frontier myth down to isolation, incomprehension, and the growth of a legend around a man who wants only to be left alone.

title: Just Because (children's book)
author: Matthew McConaughey
synopsis: A rhyming picture book built on paired opposites — 'just because' one thing is true doesn't mean another is — aimed at teaching children that people and situations hold contradictions. Short, illustrated, gift-book in tone rather than narrative.

title: Just One Look
author: Cameron Lindsay
synopsis: Probably a crime or suspense novel; I don't know this title by this author (it shares a name with Harlan Coben's 2004 thriller).

title: Land: How the Hunger for Ownership Shaped the Modern World
author: Simon Winchester
synopsis: Winchester's discursive history of land as property: how it came to be surveyed and measured, how boundaries and deeds were invented, and how ownership enabled enclosure, colonial dispossession, the Highland Clearances, apartheid-era removals, and Native American treaty-breaking. Ends on stewardship and restitution — commons, land trusts, and returns of land — and reads as linked essays rather than a single argument.

title: Let Me Finish
author: Roger Angel
synopsis: A memoir in loosely linked essays by the New Yorker writer and fiction editor Roger Angell, moving between a Manhattan boyhood in the 1920s–30s, his mother Katharine White and stepfather E.B. White, wartime service in the Pacific, magazine life, and baseball. Digressive and anecdotal rather than a continuous life story, written in his late eighties.

title: Life Is Not A Game of Perfect
author: Bob Rotalla, Ph.D.
synopsis: Golf psychologist Bob Rotella extends his mental-game coaching beyond the course, arguing that the habits that produce good golf — clear targets, commitment to a decision, indifference to outcomes, self-selected optimism — apply to careers and daily life. Built around anecdotes from tour players and business clients rather than research.

title: Lucky Jim
author: Kingsley Amis
subjects: British and irish fiction (fictional works by one author)
synopsis: Comic novel about Jim Dixon, a resentful junior lecturer in medieval history at a provincial English university, who despises his pompous department head, is entangled with a neurotic colleague, and sabotages his own prospects with drink and pratfalls. A landmark of postwar British satire on academic pretension and class.

title: Make Your Next Shot Your Best Shot: The Secret to Playing Great Golf
author: Bob Rotella, Ph.D.
synopsis: Rotella's late-career restatement of his golf psychology: play the shot in front of you, pick a target and commit, accept bad results without analysis, and separate practice-range thinking from on-course thinking. Instructional and repetitive by design, with tour-player examples; no swing mechanics.

title: Mania
author: Lionel Shriver
synopsis: Satirical novel set in an alternate 2010s America overtaken by the "Mental Parity Movement," which holds that all people are equally smart and makes noticing otherwise the last taboo; standardized tests, grades, and the word "stupid" go. Told by a professor who refuses to comply, and by her decades-long friendship-rivalry with a woman who prospers under the new creed.

title: Material World: The Six Raw Materials That Shape Modern Civilization
author: Ed Conway
synopsis: Economics journalist Ed Conway traces six substances — sand, salt, iron, copper, oil, and lithium — from mine and quarry to finished product, arguing that the modern economy's dependence on physical extraction is far larger and more fragile than digital-age rhetoric suggests. Reported travel through pits, refineries, and factories, with a running critique of GDP-based views of value.

title: Meow (The Meow Library)
author: Sam Austen
synopsis: Likely a small-format humor/gift book collecting cat photographs, quotations, or kitsch ephemera.

title: Morning After the Revolution: Dispatches From the Wrong Side of History
author: Nellie Bowles
synopsis: Essays and reporting by a former New York Times reporter on American progressive politics circa 2020–22 — Seattle's protest zone, defund-the-police, anti-racism consulting, gender medicine, homelessness policy — written in a deadpan, ironic register from inside the milieu she left. Anecdotal polemic rather than systematic argument.

title: Never Let Me Go
author: Kazuo Ishiguro
synopsis: Kathy H. recalls her upbringing at Hailsham, an isolated English boarding school, and her friendship and love triangle with Ruth and Tommy, gradually revealing that the students are clones raised to donate their organs. A restrained first-person novel about memory, resignation, and what people accept as fate.

title: North Woods: A Novel
author: Daniel Mason
synopsis: A novel told through the successive inhabitants of one house in the western Massachusetts woods across four centuries — Puritan runaways, an apple grower and his daughters, a painter, a schizophrenic man, a true-crime writer — plus letters, ballads, case notes, and the voices of trees and beetles. Its subject is ecological and human succession on a single patch of ground.

title: On Par
author: Bill Pennington
publisher: Houghton Mifflin Harcourt Trade & Reference Publishers
synopsis: A collection of pieces by the New York Times golf columnist aimed at the recreational player — etiquette, course strategy, equipment, playing partners, and the psychology of a game most people are bad at. Anecdotal and wry rather than instructional in the swing-mechanics sense.

title: On the Edge (The Art of Risking Eveything)
author: Nate Silver
synopsis: Silver maps what he calls "the River" — the interconnected world of poker players, sports bettors, venture capitalists, crypto founders, and AI risk theorists — and argues their probabilistic, expected-value style of thinking increasingly runs the culture and economy, in contrast to the credentialed consensus-driven "Village." Part reportage (poker tables, Las Vegas, SBF, Silicon Valley), part defense of calibrated risk-taking, with a long closing section on AI existential risk.

title: Our Man in Havana
author: Graham Greene
synopsis: Wormold, a hapless British vacuum-cleaner salesman in pre-revolutionary Havana, is recruited by MI6 and, needing money for his teenage daughter, invents a network of subagents and passes off sketches of vacuum parts as secret military installations — until London believes him and people start dying. Greene's satire of intelligence bureaucracies and the self-deceiving machinery of espionage.

title: Outlive
author: Peter Attia, MD
synopsis: Attia argues medicine should shift from treating disease late ("Medicine 2.0") to preventing the "Four Horsemen" — atherosclerotic disease, cancer, neurodegeneration, and metabolic dysfunction — decades in advance, with the goal of extending healthspan rather than just lifespan. The second half is tactical: aggressive lipid management, VO2 max and strength training, stability work, nutritional biochemistry, sleep, and a candid chapter on emotional health.

title: Pacific
author: Simon Winchester
synopsis: Winchester tells the story of the Pacific through loosely linked thematic episodes — U.S. nuclear testing at Bikini, the rise of Sony and consumer electronics, surfing, coral reef collapse, North Korea, typhoons, the fate of colonial empires — dated from the 1950s onward. Journalistic and digressive rather than a systematic history, ending on climate change and Chinese naval ambition.

title: Phantom Orbit
author: David Ignatius
synopsis: An Ignatius spy novel built around satellite vulnerability and space warfare: a Russian scientist who discovered a flaw in orbital navigation systems tries to make contact with the CIA, while American and Chinese intelligence services race over control of what happens above the atmosphere. Tradecraft-heavy and grounded in real defense concerns about GPS and anti-satellite weapons.

title: Piranesi
author: Susanna Clarke
synopsis: A man who calls himself Piranesi keeps a journal of life in a vast labyrinth of statue-filled halls washed by tides, worshipping the House and assisting the only other living person, "the Other" — until evidence accumulates that he has forgotten who he is and how he arrived. A short, controlled mystery about memory, captivity, and enchantment, quite unlike Clarke's Jonathan Strange in scale and voice.

title: Powers and Thrones: A New History of the Middle Ages
author: Dan Jones
synopsis: A single-volume narrative history of roughly a thousand years, from Rome's collapse to the Reformation, organized around forces and types rather than strict chronology — barbarians, Byzantines, Arabs, monks, knights, crusaders, merchants, scholars, builders, navigators, protesters. Popular history: fast, vivid, drawing frequent parallels to modern climate, migration, and pandemic anxieties rather than advancing a scholarly thesis.

title: Prisoners of Geography
author: Tim Marshall
synopsis: Marshall, a former foreign correspondent, runs through ten regions (Russia, China, the US, Western Europe, Africa, the Middle East, India/Pakistan, Korea/Japan, Latin America, the Arctic) arguing that mountains, rivers, plains, and access to warm-water ports constrain what states can do regardless of ideology or leadership. Deliberately reductive geographic determinism, useful as a primer and criticized for downplaying culture, economics, and agency.

title: Putting Out of Your Mind
author: Bob Rotella, Ph.D.
synopsis: The sports psychologist's short treatise on putting: the stroke fails mostly because of doubt and mechanical over-thinking, so the prescription is to pick a target, trust an unconscious routine, and accept missed putts without letting them alter your approach. Repetitive by design, with examples from tour players Rotella coached.

title: Recessional: The Death of Free Speech and the Cost of a Free Lunch
author: David Mamet
synopsis: A collection of short, pugnacious essays in which the playwright attacks COVID lockdowns, progressive orthodoxy in Hollywood and academia, and what he sees as a culture of enforced conformity and government handouts. Aphoristic and digressive rather than argued at length; closer to a conservative op-ed collection than a sustained thesis.

title: Red Widow
author: Alma Katsu
synopsis: A CIA-set spy novel in which analyst Lyndsey Duncan, sidelined after an affair with a British colleague, is brought back to hunt a mole in the Russia division after an asset is killed, and finds herself circling a legendary colleague known as the Red Widow. Written by a former intelligence officer, with tradecraft detail and a focus on the two women's parallel careers.

title: Reframe Your Brain / The User Interface for Happiness and Success
author: Scott Adams
synopsis: Adams argues that beliefs should be judged by whether they are useful rather than true, and offers roughly 160 short "reframes" — one-line substitute thoughts on fitness, career, money, embarrassment, persuasion, and mood — meant to be adopted like software updates. Structured as a browsable list of tips with brief commentary, not a systematic psychology.

title: Remarkably Bright Creatures: A Read with Jenna Pick
author: Shelby Van Pelt
synopsis: A debut novel alternating among Tova, a widowed woman who cleans a small-town Washington aquarium at night, a drifting young man named Cameron, and Marcellus, a giant Pacific octopus who narrates his own chapters and works out what happened to Tova's son, who vanished thirty years earlier. Sentimental, plot-driven contemporary fiction about grief and improbable friendship.

title: Return to Life Through Contrology
author: Joseph H. Pilates
synopsis: Pilates's own 1945 manual laying out "Contrology": a philosophy of whole-body health through breath, alignment, and concentration, followed by 34 mat exercises presented in sequence with photographs of Pilates demonstrating each. Short, prescriptive, and idiosyncratic — the primary source for mat Pilates as its inventor taught it.

title: Rush: Revolution, Madness, and Benjamin Rush
author: Stephen Friedman
synopsis: The metadata here is garbled; the book is almost certainly Stephen Fried's biography of Benjamin Rush, the Philadelphia physician, signer of the Declaration, and reformer who treated yellow fever, pioneered humane treatment of the mentally ill, and repaired the Adams–Jefferson friendship. A conventional, sympathetic life-and-times that argues Rush belongs among the recognized founders.

title: Seconhand Time: The Last of the Soviets
author: Svetlana Alexievich
synopsis: An oral history of the Soviet collapse assembled from hundreds of interviews, presented as unattributed monologues from ordinary people — veterans, party loyalists, refugees, suicides' relatives — about what they lost and what capitalism brought. Alexievich shapes rather than analyzes: the argument, such as it is, is that Soviet subjectivity outlived the state.

title: Shakespeare Was a Woman and Other Heresies
author: Elizabeth Winkler
synopsis: A journalist's investigation not so much of who wrote Shakespeare as of why the question is professionally forbidden, tracing the Baconian, Oxfordian, and Emilia Bassano cases while interviewing orthodox scholars and doubters. Winkler stays agnostic on authorship and argues the field's policing of the topic is itself the more interesting scandal.

title: Sidecountry: Tales of Death and Life from the Back Roads of Sports
author: John Branch
synopsis: Twenty of Branch's New York Times sports features, including the avalanche narrative "Snow Fall" and pieces on a rodeo family, hockey enforcers, and the search for missing skiers. Mostly about people at the margins of sport and about mortality rather than games or scores.

title: Silent Coup
author: Claire Provost
synopsis: Provost and Matt Kennard's reported argument that corporations have quietly captured the machinery of democracy through investor-state arbitration tribunals, special economic zones, aid-funded privatization, and private security and intelligence firms. Built from on-the-ground reporting across dozens of countries rather than theory, with a polemical framing of a legal architecture that insulates capital from voters.

title: Silverview
author: John Le Carre
synopsis: Le Carré's final completed novel, published posthumously: a London bookseller who has retreated to a East Anglian seaside town is drawn into the orbit of a Polish émigré with a mysterious past, while a Service security officer investigates a leak from within. Short and elegiac, it is less a plot-driven spy thriller than a late meditation on the moral bankruptcy of the intelligence establishment and the private loyalties that outlast institutional ones.

title: Spies of No Country / Secret Lives at the Birth of Israel
author: Matti Friedman
synopsis: Friedman recounts the true story of four Arab-born Jews recruited into the pre-state Palmach's 'Arab Section,' who posed as Arabs in Beirut and Haifa during the 1948 war. He uses their improvised, often amateurish operations to argue that Israel's origins and its intelligence culture were shaped as much by Middle Eastern Jews as by the European Zionist narrative that dominates the country's self-image.

title: Spies: The Epic Intelligence War Between East and West
author: Calder Walton
publisher: Simon & Schuster Audio and Blackstone Publishing
synopsis: A Harvard intelligence historian's sweeping survey of the espionage contest between the Soviet Union/Russia and the West from 1917 through the present, drawing on newly available archives. Walton argues the Cold War intelligence war never really ended and that the West repeatedly misread its adversaries, with China now the central target; it is long, narrative-driven, and organized chronologically around major operations and defectors.

title: Squeeze Me
author: Carl Hiaasen
synopsis: A Hiaasen comic crime novel set in Palm Beach, in which a wildlife wrangler discovers that a wealthy society matron has vanished — swallowed, it turns out, by a giant Burmese python — and the death gets spun into political propaganda by a Trumpish president wintering at his nearby club. Standard Hiaasen machinery: invasive species, Florida grotesques, and broad satire of the Mar-a-Lago set.

title: Surely You're Joking, Mr. Feynman: Adventures of a Curious Character
author: Richard P. Feynman
synopsis: A collection of anecdotes told by the Nobel-winning physicist to Ralph Leighton, covering safecracking at Los Alamos, drumming in Brazil, picking up women in bars, dismantling bureaucratic pomposity, and generally testing everything for himself. It is not a scientific autobiography but a self-portrait of a personality — curious, iconoclastic, and often self-mythologizing.

title: Adrift: America in 100 Charts
author: Scott Galloway
title_raw: Synopsis Of Adrift: America in 100 Charts
synopsis: Galloway diagnoses American decline through roughly 100 annotated charts covering wealth concentration, the cost of housing and education, corporate power, and declining social mobility. The argument is that the U.S. has shifted its economy toward protecting incumbent capital at the expense of the young; light on prose, dependent on how much you trust the data selection.

title: Target Switzerland: A Paul Muller Novel of Political Intrigue
author: William N Walker
synopsis: Apparently a self-published or small-press historical thriller in which a protagonist named Paul Muller is caught up in intrigue around Switzerland's armed neutrality and German designs on it during the Second World War.

title: Tenth of December
author: George Saunders
synopsis: Ten stories, several set in near-future or lightly speculative Americas — pharmaceutical mood experiments on prisoners, a theme park staffed by human 'lawn ornaments,' a boy and a dying man in the snow — rendered in Saunders's voice-driven, interior-monologue style. The stories pair grotesque social satire with an insistent interest in ordinary decency under economic and moral pressure.

title: The Anthropocene Reviewed: Essays on a Himan-Centered Planet
author: John Green
synopsis: Essays adapted from Green's podcast, each reviewing some facet of the human-shaped world — Canada geese, Diet Dr Pepper, the QWERTY keyboard, plague, sunsets — on a five-star scale. The conceit is a frame for personal memoir about anxiety, illness, and wonder; short, digressive, and unabashedly sentimental.

title: The 5 Love Languages: The Secret to Love That Lasts
author: Gary Chapman
synopsis: Chapman, a Baptist pastor and marriage counselor, proposes that people express and receive love primarily through one of five modes — words of affirmation, quality time, gifts, acts of service, physical touch — and that most marital friction comes from partners speaking different ones. Built on counseling anecdotes rather than research, with exercises and a self-assessment quiz.

title: The Anomaly
author: Herve le Tellier
synopsis: An Air France flight from Paris to New York hits violent turbulence and lands twice — once in March, once again in June — with two physically identical sets of passengers and crew, forcing governments, scientists and theologians to confront what the duplication means. Le Tellier braids thriller, comedy and metaphysical puzzle (with a nod to the simulation hypothesis) through a dozen character portraits; it won the 2020 Prix Goncourt.

title: The Art of Looking: How to Read Modern and Contemporary Art
author: Lance Esplund
synopsis: Art critic Lance Esplund makes the case that modern and contemporary art rewards patient, first-hand looking rather than wall labels, theory or market gossip, and then models that looking in short essays on individual works and artists (Matisse, Rothko, Johns, Bourgeois, Kiefer, Sherman and others). Practical and opinionated — he freely judges some celebrated work as empty — it is closer to a training in attention than a survey of art history.

title: The Art Thief
author: Michael Finkel
synopsis: Narrative nonfiction about Stéphane Breitwieser, who with his girlfriend stole roughly 300 works from small European museums and churches in the 1990s, keeping them in his mother's attic rather than selling them. Finkel reconstructs the thefts and the investigation while probing Breitwieser's claim that he stole out of love of beauty, and the catastrophic fate of the collection after his arrest.

title: The Biggest Bluff
author: Maria Konnikava
synopsis: Psychologist and journalist Maria Konnikova (spelled Konnikova) sets out to learn no-limit hold'em from scratch under pro Erik Seidel, using the game as a laboratory for how people misjudge luck, skill and control. Part tournament memoir, part popular decision science, drawing on von Neumann, Kahneman and her own bankroll.

title: The Bogey Man: A Month on the PGA Tour
author: George Plimpton
synopsis: Plimpton's participatory-journalism account of playing as a hopeless amateur in West Coast pro-am tournaments alongside touring pros in the mid-1960s. It is as much a collection of caddie lore, golfers' superstitions and clubhouse anecdote as a chronicle of his own escalating yips.

title: The Boys from Biloxi: A Legal Thriller
author: John Grisham
synopsis: Grisham's legal thriller follows two boyhood friends in Biloxi, Mississippi, sons of Croatian immigrants — one the child of a district attorney, the other of the local crime boss who runs the Gulf Coast's strip joints and casinos — whose paths diverge into prosecution and mob defense. Spanning several decades, it builds toward a capital murder trial pitting the two families against each other.

title: The Bunker Game: How to Play with Confidence from the Sand
author: David Armitage
synopsis: Presumably a golf instruction manual on sand play — bunker technique, club selection and course management from awkward lies.

title: The Code Breaker
author: Jennifer Doudna
synopsis: Note: this is Walter Isaacson's biography of Jennifer Doudna, not a book by her. It traces Doudna's path from RNA structural biology to the CRISPR gene-editing breakthrough, her patent and priority rivalry with Feng Zhang's lab, the Nobel with Emmanuelle Charpentier, and the ethical fight over editing human embryos, ending with CRISPR-based COVID testing.

title: The Devil's Chessboard
author: David Talbot
synopsis: A hostile biography of Allen Dulles, arguing that as OSS officer and CIA director he built a largely unaccountable secret government — shielding Nazi assets and personnel, running coups in Iran and Guatemala, and defying Kennedy after the Bay of Pigs. Talbot goes on to argue, on circumstantial grounds, that Dulles and his circle were implicated in or complicit around the JFK assassination and its cover-up, which is where most critics part company with him.

title: The Disenlightenment (Polits, Horror and Entertainment)
author: David Mamet
synopsis: Most likely a collection of Mamet's late-career polemical essays on politics, Hollywood, culture and Jewish identity, continuing the contrarian conservative line of Recessional and Everywhere an Oink Oink.

title: The Dumbest Generation: How the Digital Age Stupefies Young Americans and Jeopardizes our Future
author: Mark Bauerlein
synopsis: Emory English professor Mark Bauerlein marshals survey and test data (NAEP, NEA reading studies, employer complaints) to argue that Americans under 30 have unprecedented access to information and unprecedented ignorance of history, civics, and literature, because screen habits crowd out sustained reading and adult mentorship in favor of peer chatter. A polemic against techno-optimism in education, weakest where it treats correlation and generational anecdote as proof.

title: The End of The Myth
author: Greg Grandin
synopsis: Grandin recasts American history around the frontier as ideological safety valve: expansion abroad and westward let the country defer reckoning with racism, class conflict, and its own violence. He traces the line from Indian removal, the Mexican War, and Jim Crow through Cold War interventions and NAFTA to the border wall, which he reads as the frontier myth's collapse into a politics of walls and grievance.

title: The Fatal Shore: The Epic of Australia's Founding
author: Robert Hughes
synopsis: A narrative history of Australia's convict transportation system from 1787 to the 1860s, built on trial records, letters, and convict testimony, covering the First Fleet, the penal hells of Norfolk Island and Macquarie Harbour, floggings, escape, sexuality, and Aboriginal dispossession. Hughes argues the convict past shaped Australian character and was long suppressed as a national shame — vivid, literary, and criticized by academic historians for its darkness and dramatic license.

title: The Fire Above, the Mountain Below (The German List) Translated from German by Wieland Hoban
author: Reinhard Jirgl
synopsis: Likely a novel by the East German-born experimentalist Reinhard Jirgl, written in his idiosyncratic typographically fractured German prose, published in English by Seagull Books' German List in Wieland Hoban's translation.

title: The Foundations of Winning Golf
author: Jon Sherman
synopsis: Probably a variant title or edition of Jon Sherman's "The Four Foundations of Golf," the Practical Golf author's data-informed guide to expectations, course strategy, practice structure, and technique.

title: The Four Foundations of Golf: How to Build a Game That Lastat a Lifetime
author: Jon Sherman
synopsis: Sherman, who runs the Practical Golf site, argues most amateurs improve fastest by fixing four things other than their swing: realistic expectations about scoring, smarter course strategy and shot selection, deliberate practice with feedback, and only then technique. Leans on strokes-gained and shot-tracking research (Broadie, Arccos) to explain why chasing a perfect swing wastes most golfers' time.

title: The Ghost Map
author: Steven Johnson
synopsis: Johnson reconstructs London's 1854 Broad Street cholera outbreak and how physician John Snow and curate Henry Whitehead traced it to a single water pump, overturning miasma theory with the famous dot map and door-to-door evidence. He uses the case to argue for cities as engines of knowledge and for mapping and data as tools of epidemiology, with digressions on urban density, waste, and modern pandemic risk.

title: The Glitter in the Green: In Search of Hummingbirds
author: Jon Dunn
synopsis: Naturalist Jon Dunn travels the Americas from Alaska to Tierra del Fuego chasing hummingbirds, mixing field observation of their extreme physiology and behavior with the human history around them: Aztec symbolism, Victorian skin collectors and feather fashion, taxonomic obsessives, and present-day conservation and ecotourism.

title: The Gold Bug Variations
author: Richard Powers
synopsis: A double-helix novel: in 1957 a young molecular biologist, Stuart Ressler, abandons science after a failed romance and the race to crack the genetic code; twenty-five years later a librarian and an art historian try to reconstruct his story. Powers braids genetics, Bach's Goldberg Variations, information theory, and love into a dense meditation on codes, coding, and what it costs to keep learning.

title: The Golf of Your Dreams
author: Bob Rotalla, Ph.D.
synopsis: Sports psychologist Bob Rotella's guide to the mental side of golf, arguing that scoring comes from a confident, target-focused, non-analytical mindset — routine, short-game commitment, and accepting bad shots — rather than swing mechanics. Structured as a course of instruction with drills and anecdotes from his tour clients.

title: The Golfer's Guide to the Meaning of Life: Lessons I've Learned from My Life on the Links
author: Gary Player
synopsis: South African golf legend Gary Player pairs anecdotes from his tournament career with short essays on discipline, fitness, faith, family and integrity, using golf as a vehicle for conventional character advice. It's a memoir-flavored inspirational book rather than an instructional or technical golf text.

title: The Golfer's Mind
author: Bob Rotella, Ph.D.
synopsis: Sports psychologist Bob Rotella distills his coaching into short, repetitive chapters on the mental habits of good players: committing fully to each shot, staying process-focused, accepting bad results, and thinking without fear on the course. Written as a set of reminders to be reread rather than a systematic argument, and aimed at competitive and serious amateur golfers.

title: The Great Reset and the Struggle for Liberty: Unraveling the Global Agenda
author: Michael Rectenwald
synopsis: Rectenwald, a former NYU professor turned right-libertarian critic, argues that the World Economic Forum's "Great Reset" and stakeholder capitalism amount to a corporatist-socialist project that concentrates power and erodes individual liberty, examining ESG, COVID policy, transhumanism and Fourth Industrial Revolution rhetoric. The book takes WEF publications largely at face value as evidence of a coordinated elite agenda.

title: The Hero with a Thousand Faces
author: Joseph Campbell
synopsis: Campbell's comparative-mythology classic argues that hero myths worldwide share a single underlying pattern—the "monomyth" of departure, initiation and return—and reads it psychologically, via Freud and Jung, as a map of inner transformation. Enormously influential on writers and screenwriters, though scholars fault its selective, universalizing use of sources.

title: The Inner Game of Golf
author: Timothy W. Gallwey
synopsis: Gallwey applies his "Inner Game" framework—quieting the interfering, judging "Self 1" so the body's natural learning "Self 2" can perform—to golf, using attention exercises, awareness drills rather than mechanical instruction, and accounts of his own students. Aimed at players whose swing collapses under self-conscious over-thinking.

title: The Key Muscles of Yoga: Scientific Keys, Volume I
author: Ray Long, MD
synopsis: An anatomy manual for yoga practitioners and teachers, with detailed color illustrations of the muscles, bones and joint actions involved in standard hatha postures, organized by muscle group and by pose. Long, an orthopedic surgeon, emphasizes concepts like agonist/antagonist action and facilitated stretching to explain how alignment cues work biomechanically.

title: The Last Cowboys
author: John Branch
