synopsis: New York Times reporter John Branch follows Bill Wright and his sons, a southern Utah ranching family who compete at the top of professional saddle bronc riding, across several rodeo seasons of injuries, drought and land pressures. It's narrative nonfiction about the economics and physical cost of a vanishing Western way of life.

title: The Last Days of Night
author: Graham Moore
synopsis: A historical novel in which young lawyer Paul Cravath defends George Westinghouse against Thomas Edison's billion-dollar patent suit over the light bulb, moving through the War of the Currents, Nikola Tesla, and Gilded Age New York. Moore freely rearranges the real chronology, as he explains in an afterword.

title: The Little Book of Talent: 52 Tips for Improving Your Skills
author: Daniel Coyle
synopsis: A practical companion to Coyle's The Talent Code, offering 52 short tips organized around igniting motivation, improving practice, and sustaining progress—things like practicing in slow motion, embracing struggle, and using "deep practice" reps. Prescriptive and skimmable, with the underlying myelin/skill-circuit research kept in the background.

title: The Looming Tower / Al-Qaeda and The Road to 9/11
author: Lawrence Wright
synopsis: A narrative history of al-Qaeda's rise, tracing the ideological lineage from Sayyid Qutb through Ayman al-Zawahiri and Osama bin Laden, and interleaving it with the story of FBI counterterrorism chief John O'Neill and the bureaucratic rivalries (especially FBI-CIA) that left the 9/11 plot undetected. Built on hundreds of interviews; won the Pulitzer for general nonfiction.

title: The Mandibles
author: Lionel Shriver
subjects: Successions et héritages -- Romans, nouvelles, etc
synopsis: A near-future satirical novel (subtitled "A Family, 2029-2047") in which a US sovereign default and hyperinflation wipe out four generations of a well-off New York family's expected inheritance. Shriver uses the family's slide into scarcity and improvised survival to argue polemically about debt, entitlement, and monetary policy.

title: The Master: The Long Run and Beautiful Game of Roger Federer
author: Christopher Clarey
synopsis: A biography of Roger Federer by the longtime New York Times tennis correspondent, drawn from decades of interviews with Federer, his coaches, and rivals. Organized around key matches and turning points, it treats his technique, business self-management, and the Nadal/Djokovic rivalries rather than offering intimate personal revelation.

title: The Money Plot
author: Frederick Kaufman
synopsis: Kaufman argues that money is essentially a story-telling and metaphor-making technology, tracing it from ancient tokens and sacrificial accounting through coins, credit, and modern derivatives. A journalist's cultural-anthropological account of finance as fiction, more interpretive essay than economic history.

title: The Motion of the Body Through Space
author: Lionel Shriver
synopsis: A novel about a sedentary sixty-something man who abruptly announces he will run a marathon and then escalates to an extreme triathlon, narrated largely through the exasperation of his wife, a personal trainer. Shriver satirizes endurance-sport fanaticism as a substitute religion, with a caustic subplot about diversity mandates at the husband's former employer.

title: The New Encyclopedia of Modern Bodybuilding: The Bible of Bodybuilding
author: Arnold Schwarzenegger
synopsis: An 800-page reference manual covering bodybuilding history, anatomy and muscle-by-muscle exercise catalogs, graduated training programs from beginner to competition level, nutrition, injury management, and posing and contest preparation, illustrated with archival photos. Includes Schwarzenegger's own training story, though the physiology and drug discussion reflects 1990s thinking.

title: The New Map - Energy, Climate, And The Clash of Nations
author: Daniel Yergin
synopsis: Yergin's survey of twenty-first-century energy geopolitics: the American shale revolution, Russia's pipeline leverage, China's Belt and Road and South China Sea ambitions, Middle Eastern realignment, and the coming of electric vehicles and decarbonization. Reportorial and map-by-map rather than argumentative, ending with a cautious assessment of how fast an energy transition can happen.

title: The Nineties: A Book
author: Chuck Klosterman
synopsis: An essayistic cultural history of the decade between the fall of the Berlin Wall and 9/11, covering Nirvana and authenticity, Ross Perot and Clinton, Seinfeld and Titanic, the arrival of the internet, and the O.J. and election-recount spectacles. Klosterman's thesis is that the nineties were the last era of mediated-but-analog experience, when detachment and irony were the default posture.

title: The Official Old's Cool Education II - Just Do Wit Education (johnnymustard.com)
synopsis: Apparently a self-published miscellany/almanac of "old-fashioned" practical knowledge, quizzes, and life lessons, marketed as a family education gift book.

title: The Old Man
author: Thomas Perry
synopsis: A thriller about Dan Chase, a retired intelligence operative who has lived under false identities for decades after absconding with cash meant for a Libyan warlord, and who must run again when both his old agency and foreign assassins locate him. Procedural and tradecraft-heavy; adapted into the FX series with Jeff Bridges.

title: The Outsider: Albert M. Greenfield and the Fall of the Protestant Establishment
author: Dan Rottenberg
subjects: HISTORY / United States / State & Local / Middle Atlantic (DC, DE, MD, NJ, NY, PA)
synopsis: A biography of Albert M. Greenfield (1887–1967), a Ukrainian-Jewish immigrant who became Philadelphia's dominant real estate broker, banker, and department-store owner, surviving a bank collapse in the Depression and reinventing himself as a political power broker. Rottenberg uses Greenfield's career as a lens on how an outsider battered the city's insular WASP elite, and on the personal costs and ethical compromises involved.

title: The Overstory
author: Richard Powers
synopsis: A novel in which nine loosely linked Americans—an artist, a scientist, a paraplegic coder, an activist student, and others—are drawn into the fate of North America's old-growth forests, some of them into radical eco-sabotage. Powers structures the book like a tree (roots, trunk, crown, seeds) and argues, in fiction, that trees are communicating, cooperating beings on a timescale humans can barely perceive.

title: The Overstory
author: Richard Powers
synopsis: Same book as above: Powers's Pulitzer-winning novel that braids nine human stories into a single narrative about old-growth forests, tree science, and environmental activism that shades into sabotage. Ambitious and didactic in places; the human characters largely serve the argument about arboreal time and interdependence.

title: The Paladin: A Spy Novel
author: David Ignatius
synopsis: A thriller in which disgraced CIA officer Michael Dunne, jailed after an off-books operation against a journalist collective in Italy, comes out of prison hunting the people who set him up. Ignatius builds the plot around disinformation, deepfakes, and the blurred line between hacking journalists and hacking the truth.

title: The Personal Librarian
author: Marie Benedict
synopsis: A historical novel by Marie Benedict and Victoria Christopher Murray about Belle da Costa Greene, the librarian who built J. P. Morgan's collection and ran the Morgan Library, and who lived her adult life as a white woman of Portuguese descent while being the daughter of Black activist Richard Greener. The book dramatizes her rise in the rare-book world alongside the constant threat of exposure.

title: The Philadelphia Music Book: Sounds of a City
author: Larry Magid
synopsis: Likely an illustrated survey of Philadelphia's popular music history—Philly soul, doo-wop, American Bandstand, rock venues—assembled with concert promoter Larry Magid, but I can't confirm its contents.

title: The Port Huron Statement
author: Richard Flacks
synopsis: An edited collection (with Nelson Lichtenstein) of essays revisiting the 1962 SDS manifesto: its intellectual sources, its drafting by Tom Hayden and the early SDS circle, and its afterlife in feminism, labor, and later left politics. Scholarly and retrospective rather than a straight reprint, though the Statement itself is included.

title: The Psychology of Money
author: Morgan Housel
synopsis: Nineteen short essays arguing that financial outcomes depend less on technical knowledge than on behavior—ego, envy, patience, tolerance for volatility, and the role of luck. Housel's practical thrust is toward saving, room for error, compounding over long horizons, and defining "enough"; it's anecdote-driven rather than data-heavy.

title: The Puzzler
author: A.J. Jacobs
synopsis: Jacobs tours the world of puzzles—crosswords, anagrams, jigsaws, Rubik's cubes, mazes, Japanese logic puzzles, chess problems—meeting champions and constructors and trying (badly) to compete himself. Interspersed with actual puzzles for the reader, and a running argument that puzzle-solving habits sharpen how we approach real problems.

title: The Secret Hours
author: Mick Herron
synopsis: A standalone set in Herron's Slough House world: a politically motivated inquiry into historical MI5 misconduct, staffed by people meant to find nothing, stumbles onto a buried operation in 1990s Berlin. The novel alternates between the present-day bureaucratic farce and the Berlin case, and quietly supplies origin material for a key Slough House figure.

title: The Shipping News
author: Annie Proulx
synopsis: Quoyle, a hapless, humiliated newspaperman from upstate New York, returns with his two daughters and an aunt to his ancestral Newfoundland outport after his unfaithful wife's death, and finds a wary footing writing the shipping news and car-wreck stories for a local paper. Proulx tells it in clipped, sentence-fragment prose thick with weather, boats, and knot lore; it won the Pulitzer and National Book Award.

title: The Signature of All Things: A Novel
author: Elizabeth Gilbert
synopsis: Gilbert's 2013 novel follows Alma Whittaker, daughter of a self-made botanical-trade magnate in Philadelphia, from the 1800s through a life of bryology, thwarted desire, and an eventual theory of natural selection she never publishes. It's a deliberately old-fashioned 19th-century-style novel about science, faith, and a woman's intellectual ambition, ranging from Peru to Tahiti to Amsterdam.

title: The Sixth Extinction: An Unnatural History
author: Elizabeth Kolbert
publisher: Simon & Schuster Audio and Blackstone Publishing
synopsis: Kolbert reports from field sites—Panamanian frog labs, the Great Barrier Reef, Amazon forest plots, an acidified island off Italy—to argue that human activity is driving a mass extinction comparable to the five in the geological record. She interleaves the history of how scientists came to accept extinction and catastrophism at all; winner of the 2015 Pulitzer for general nonfiction.

title: The Talent Code: Greatness Isn't Born. It's Grown. Here's How.
author: Daniel Coyle
synopsis: Coyle visits "talent hotbeds" (Brazilian futsal courts, a Moscow tennis club, a Dallas music school) and builds a three-part theory of skill: deep practice at the edge of ability, motivational "ignition," and master coaching. The proposed mechanism is myelin insulation thickening around heavily fired neural circuits—a popular-science framing that has since been criticized as oversimplified.

title: The Tao of Deception
author: Ralph D. Sawyer
synopsis: Sawyer, a translator of the classical Chinese military texts, surveys the theory and practice of deception in Chinese warfare from the Warring States through the twentieth century, organized around concepts like the orthodox/unorthodox (zheng/qi) pairing, feints, disinformation, and estimation. Dense and heavily sourced in primary texts rather than a popular strategy guide.

title: The Ultimate Round: Pebble Beach Golf Links
author: Neal Hotelling

title: The Undoing Project: A Friendship That Changed Our Minds
author: Michael Lewis
synopsis: Lewis tells the story of Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky—their Israeli backgrounds, wartime service, and combustible collaboration—and how their work on heuristics and biases undermined the assumption of human rationality in economics. It's a double biography of a friendship as much as an explainer of prospect theory and the judgment research behind behavioral economics.

title: The Universe in Verse: 15 Portals to Wonder through Science & Poetry (for Julia)
author: Maria Popova
synopsis: Popova's print outgrowth of her live Universe in Verse show: fifteen chapters, each pairing a poem with an essay on a scientific idea or figure (from the discovery of Saturn's rings to Rachel Carson and the Voyager record), illustrated by Ofra Amit. Short, lyrical, and closer to a gift-book meditation on wonder than to science writing proper.

title: The Unstoppable Golfer
author: Bob Rotella, Ph.D.
synopsis: Sports psychologist Rotella's advice on playing golf without fear or self-consciousness—getting to a state of automatic, present-tense play, with heavy emphasis on attitude around the short game and putting. Anecdote-driven and repetitive of his earlier books, aimed at amateurs who fall apart under pressure.

title: The World for Sale: Money, Power, and the Traders Who Barter the Earth's Resources
author: Javier Blas
synopsis: Blas and Jack Farchy, both Bloomberg commodities reporters, chronicle the secretive traders—Philipp Brothers, Marc Rich, Vitol, Glencore, Trafigura, Cargill—who move oil, metals, and grain, and the deals they cut with sanctioned regimes, dictators, and post-Soviet states. It argues these firms have wielded quiet geopolitical power for decades while operating largely outside public scrutiny.

title: The Year of Lear, Shakespeare in 1606
author: James Shapiro
synopsis: Shapiro reconstructs a single year in Shakespeare's working life, arguing that King Lear, Macbeth, and Antony and Cleopatra were shaped by the aftermath of the Gunpowder Plot, James I's push to unite England and Scotland, plague closures, and public controversies over equivocation, demonic possession, and royal succession. A literary-historical companion to his 1599, more concerned with political atmosphere than biography.

title: They All Saw A Cat
author: Brenda Wenzel
synopsis: A picture book (author/illustrator Brendan Wenzel) in which the same cat walks through the world and is seen utterly differently by a child, a dog, a fish, a bee, a bat, a worm, and others, each rendered in a different visual style. A Caldecott Honor book that teaches perspective and sensory difference through pictures rather than explanation.

title: Things That Go Bump in the Universe: How Astronomers Decode Cosmic Chaos
author: C. Renee James
synopsis: A popular-science account of transient and violent astronomy — supernovae, gamma-ray bursts, fast radio bursts, colliding neutron stars, gravitational waves — tracing how astronomers moved from viewing a fixed sky to monitoring one that constantly explodes and changes. James emphasizes the instruments, surveys, and human detective work behind each discovery.

title: Touch
author: Olaf Olafsson
synopsis: A quiet Icelandic novel in which a retired Reykjavík restaurateur, idle during the COVID lockdown, receives an unexpected message and sets off for Japan to find the woman he loved in 1960s London, whose family vanished without explanation. Olafsson interleaves memory and travel toward a late revelation about why she disappeared.

title: Train Dreams: A Novella
author: Denis Johnson
synopsis: A short novel following Robert Grainier, an orphaned day laborer in the Idaho panhandle in the early twentieth century, who works railroad bridge and logging crews and loses his wife and infant daughter to a wildfire. Compressed, elegiac, and touched with the uncanny, it uses one unremarkable life to register the closing of the American frontier.

title: Transit Tourism: The Iconic Art and Design of 22 Subway Systems around the World
author: David Seltzer
synopsis: Apparently an illustrated survey of the architecture, signage, tilework, and graphic identity of twenty-two metro systems worldwide, organized city by city.

title: Tree of Smoke: A Novel
author: Dennis Johnson
synopsis: A sprawling Vietnam-era novel (by Denis Johnson) tracking CIA operative Skip Sands and his mythic uncle the Colonel through psychological-operations schemes, alongside the doomed Houston brothers, a Canadian nurse, and Vietnamese double agents, from 1963 into the war's aftermath. Its subject is intelligence work as self-deception and the moral fog of American empire; winner of the 2007 National Book Award.

title: Trust
author: Herman Diaz
synopsis: By Hernan Diaz: four nested documents about the same 1920s Wall Street fortune — a roman à clef about a financier and his wife, the tycoon's self-serving unfinished memoir, the recollections of the ghostwriter he hired to correct the record, and the wife's private notebooks. The structure argues that money buys authorship of the past, and that a woman's intelligence was written out of the story.

title: Undaunted Courage: Meriweather Lewis, Thomas Jefferson and the Opening of the American West
author: Stephen Ambrose
synopsis: A narrative biography of Meriwether Lewis built around the 1804–06 expedition, drawing heavily on the explorers' journals to cover Jefferson's ambitions, the Corps of Discovery's crossing to the Pacific, encounters with Native nations, and Lewis's decline and suicide. Popular, admiring history; strong on logistics and adventure, and criticized for its uncritical view of expansion.

title: Undermoney
author: Jay Newman
synopsis: A financial thriller by a former Elliott Management sovereign-debt investor, in which a hedge-fund manager, a special-ops veteran, and Russian and Washington power players maneuver over vast pools of untraceable capital used to buy political outcomes. Its interest lies less in the plotting than in the insider detail about how large money actually moves.

title: Very Important People: Status and Beauty in the Global Party Circuit
author: Ashley Mears
synopsis: Mears, a sociologist and former fashion model, spent 18 months as a participant-observer in VIP nightclubs in New York, Miami, Saint-Tropez and beyond, tracking how club promoters recruit young women whose beauty functions as capital. She argues that the party circuit is a labor market in which women's bodies are converted into status and business connections for rich men, while the women themselves are paid mostly in drinks, travel, and the promise of belonging.

title: What Do You Care What Other People Think: Further Adventures of a Curious Character
author: Richard P. Feynman
subjects: United States. Presidential Commission on the Space Shuttle Challenger Accident
synopsis: A second collection of Feynman's told-to-Ralph-Leighton reminiscences, lighter on pranks than 'Surely You're Joking' and centered on his relationship with his first wife Arlene, who died of tuberculosis while he was at Los Alamos. The second half is a long, documented account of his work on the Rogers Commission investigating the Challenger explosion, including his O-ring demonstration and his suppressed dissenting appendix on NASA's risk estimates.

title: When China Ruled the Seas
author: Louise Levathes
synopsis: A narrative history of the early Ming 'treasure fleets' of the eunuch admiral Zheng He, whose enormous ships sailed to Southeast Asia, India, Arabia and East Africa between 1405 and 1433. Levathes reconstructs the voyages from Chinese sources and explains the court politics and Confucian-bureaucratic reaction that led China to abandon and dismantle its navy just as Europe began expanding.

title: Who is Maud Dixon
author: Alexandra Andrews
synopsis: A literary thriller in which Florence Darrow, a failed young publishing assistant, becomes assistant to a reclusive bestselling novelist writing as 'Maud Dixon,' then sees an opening to steal her identity after a car crash in Morocco. The novel plays with autofiction, class envy, and unreliable narration as the two women maneuver against each other.

title: Why we Sleep
author: Matthew Walker, Ph.D
synopsis: A neuroscientist's popular survey of sleep research: sleep architecture and circadian rhythms, the roles of REM and NREM in memory and emotion, and the claimed consequences of short sleep for Alzheimer's, cancer, immunity, obesity and accidents. Persuasive as advocacy but criticized for overstating and occasionally misreporting the underlying evidence, so read it alongside the published critiques.

title: Why You Suck at Golf: 50 Most Common Mistakes by Recreational Golfers
author: Clive Scarff
synopsis: An instructional golf book cataloguing fifty frequent amateur errors—setup, grip, alignment, swing faults, club selection, course management—with short diagnoses and fixes rather than a single swing system. Aimed at self-taught recreational players; independently published and light on technical depth.

title: Win Bigly: Persuasion in a World Where Facts Don't Matter
author: Scott Adams
synopsis: The Dilbert cartoonist, who publicly predicted Trump's 2016 win, argues that Trump succeeded as a 'Master Persuader' using techniques from hypnosis and marketing—anchoring, visual language, strategic exaggeration, provoking opponents into reaction—and that humans are irrational creatures whose 'movies in their heads' matter more than facts. Part persuasion primer, part self-congratulatory memoir of Adams's own blogging predictions.

title: Woke Racism
author: John McWhorter
synopsis: McWhorter, a linguist, argues that contemporary anti-racist ideology of the Kendi/DiAngelo variety functions as a religion—with original sin, clergy, heresy and no path to absolution—rather than as a political program, and that it is condescending toward and harmful to Black Americans. He proposes alternative priorities (phonics-based reading instruction, ending the war on drugs, vocational education) and tactics for resisting the ideology's social enforcement.

title: You Can't Joke About That
author: Kat Timpf
synopsis: A Fox News personality and stand-up comic's case against censoring comedy, mixing free-speech argument with memoir about her mother's death, bombing on stage, and being shouted down at shows. Aimed at readers sympathetic to the anti-cancel-culture position; more polemic and personal essay than analysis.

title: Your 15th Club: The Inner Secret to Great Golf
author: Bob Rotella, Ph.D.
synopsis: Sports psychologist Rotella argues that a golfer's mind is the '15th club'—the one that determines whether the other fourteen work—and lays out routines for committing to a target, accepting outcomes, and playing with confidence and 'small' focus. Drawn largely from work with tour professionals, with anecdotes as instruction rather than swing mechanics.

title: Zilot & Other Important Rhymes
author: Bob Odenkirk
synopsis: A collection of short, silly poems Odenkirk wrote for and with his children over many years, illustrated by his daughter Erin Odenkirk. It's a kids' verse book in the Silverstein/Prelutsky vein — invented words, monsters, bedtime complaints — not a comedy memoir or anything to do with his acting career.

title: Suicidal Empathy: Dying to be Kind
author: Gad Saad
title_raw: Sucidal Empathy: Dying to be Kind
synopsis: Saad's follow-up to The Parasitic Mind, built around his coined term "suicidal empathy": the claim that compassion untempered by reason becomes self-destructive at the societal level, applied chiefly to immigration, crime policy, and identity politics in the West. Expect the same evolutionary-psychology framing and combative op-ed tone rather than new empirical research.

title: Shipwreck! Winslow Homer and The Life Line
author: Kathy Foster
synopsis: A short, focused art-historical study (published with a Philadelphia Museum of Art exhibition) of Winslow Homer's 1884 painting The Life Line, tracing its sources in shipwreck imagery, rescue technology, and popular illustration, and using X-radiography and preparatory drawings to reconstruct how Homer revised the composition — famously painting out the rescuer's face. Best suited to readers interested in a single-picture case study of Homer's method.

title: The Parasitic Mind: How Infectious Ideas Are Killing Common Sense
author: Gad Saad
publisher: Regnery Publishing, Incorporated, An Eagle Publishing Company
synopsis: Saad, a marketing professor and evolutionary behavioral scientist, argues that "idea pathogens" — postmodernism, radical feminism, social constructivism, identity politics — spread through universities and media and erode people's capacity for reason, and he prescribes free speech and evolutionary science as the cure. Polemical and anecdote-driven, drawing heavily on his own campus and online battles rather than systematic evidence.

title: Picturepedia: An Encyclopedia on Every Page (Sent to the kids)
author: DK
synopsis: A large-format DK visual reference for children (roughly ages 8–12) covering science, nature, history, space, culture and technology, with each spread built as a densely annotated infographic page rather than continuous text. Designed for browsing and homework lookups, not reading through.

title: Redwood: The Untold Story of the Cold War's Most Extraordinary Spy
author: Ben Macintyre

title: Life Is Not A Game of Perfect
author: Bob Rotalla, Ph.D.
synopsis: The sports psychologist's sequel to Golf Is Not a Game of Perfect, transferring his golf mental-game principles — confident self-talk, process over outcome, accepting bad breaks, defining your own goals — to work, business, and everyday decisions. Short essayistic chapters heavy on client anecdotes; thin on new material if you've read his golf books.

title: The Golf of Your Dreams
author: Bob Rotalla, Ph.D.
synopsis: Rotella's practical improvement program for serious amateurs: how to practice with purpose, build and trust a pre-shot routine, prioritize the short game and scoring, and manage expectations over a season of golf. More instructional and structured than his motivational bestsellers.

title: How Champions Think: In Sports and in Life
author: Bob Rotella, Ph.D.
synopsis: Rotella distills what he has observed in elite golfers and other athletes into a set of habits of mind — self-selected optimism, exclusive attention to what you control, indifference to others' opinions, tolerance for the grind — and argues these are learned rather than innate, with applications beyond sport. Anecdote-based coaching philosophy, not research psychology.

title: Make Your Next Shot Your Best Shot: The Secret to Playing Great Golf
author: Bob Rotella, Ph.D.
synopsis: Late-career Rotella book organized around the discipline of treating every shot as fresh: letting go of the previous swing, committing fully to a decision, and staying in a shot-by-shot routine rather than tracking score or outcome. Same core doctrine as Golf Is Not a Game of Perfect, restated with newer tour anecdotes.

title: Putting Out of Your Mind
author: Bob Rotella, Ph.D.
synopsis: Rotella applies his sports-psychology approach specifically to putting, arguing that good putting comes from confidence, a consistent routine, and reacting to a picked target rather than thinking about stroke mechanics. Short chapters mix tour-player anecdotes with drills and games meant to build trust in your stroke and indifference to results.

title: The Unstoppable Golfer
author: Bob Rotella, Ph.D.
synopsis: Rotella's later book on reaching a mental state where nothing—bad breaks, pressure, missed shots—derails you, with heavy emphasis on scoring clubs, wedge play, and putting. Draws on his work with players like Pádraig Harrington, Darren Clarke, and Keegan Bradley to argue that the difference between good and great is attitude and commitment to a process, not swing technique.

title: Your 15th Club: The Inner Secret to Great Golf
author: Bob Rotella, Ph.D.
synopsis: Rotella's premise is that the mind is the golfer's fifteenth club and the one most players never practice: he covers self-image, patience, dreaming big, and managing expectations over a round and a season. Largely a restatement and extension of his earlier themes with newer tour anecdotes.

title: Golf is Not a Game of Perfect
author: Bob Rotella, Ph.D.
synopsis: Rotella's best-known book and the founding text of modern golf mental coaching: it argues that golf rewards players who accept imperfect ball-striking, commit fully to a target, and keep an unshakable pre-shot routine and short memory. Built from his work with tour pros, with chapters on confidence, course management, and practicing the short game rather than chasing swing perfection.

title: The Golfer's Mind
author: Bob Rotella, Ph.D.
synopsis: A handbook-style distillation of Rotella's teaching, organized as dozens of short chapters on specific topics—first tee nerves, slumps, practice habits, playing in wind, competing—meant to be dipped into rather than read straight through. Little new theory beyond his earlier books; the value is the reference format.

title: Golf Is A Game of Confidence
author: Bob Rotella, Ph.D.
synopsis: The sequel to Golf Is Not a Game of Perfect, focused on where confidence comes from and how players build and protect it: selective memory, positive self-talk, realistic goals, and treating practice as confidence-building rather than fault-finding. Structured around case studies of tour and amateur players, with some extension of the ideas to work and life.

title: Dave Pelz's Short Game Bible: Master the Finesse Swing and Lower Your Score
author: Dave Pelz
synopsis: Pelz's data-driven case that most strokes are lost inside 100 yards, presenting his research on wedge play, chipping, pitching, sand and lob shots. The core method is the "finesse swing" and a three-lever/four-wedge "clock system" for controlling distance, plus measurement-based practice routines and diagnostics.

title: Golf In The Kingdom
author: Michael Murphy
synopsis: A semi-autobiographical novel by the co-founder of Esalen about an evening round and long night at the fictional Scottish links of Burningbush with a mystic club pro, Shivas Irons. The first half is narrative; the second is essays and notes treating golf as a discipline for exploring consciousness, body awareness, and the mystical—more countercultural philosophy than instruction.

title: The Ultimate Round: Pebble Beach Golf Links
author: Neal Hotelling
synopsis: Likely a photographic and historical hole-by-hole treatment of Pebble Beach Golf Links by the resort's longtime historian, covering the course's design, championships, and lore.
